title: Male Reproductive System Anatomy: Testes, Ducts & Gland
description: Explore male reproductive system anatomy, including the testes, epididymis, ductus deferens, seminal vesicles, prostate gland, urethra, and external parts.
h1: Male Reproductive System Anatomy: Testes, Ducts and Glands
blurb: Temperature-regulated testes, coiled epididymal maturation ducts, muscular vas deferens, accessory glands, and the shared urogenital tract in complete context.
lead: The male reproductive system combines external temperature-regulated gonads with an internal network of muscular ducts and secretory glands built to mature and transport gametes. In this illustrated guide to male reproductive system anatomy, we examine 20 documented structures—including testis & seminiferous tubules, epididymis, vas deferens, seminal vesicle—linking regional topography, tissue architecture, physiological mechanisms, and clinical reasoning.
overview: The male reproductive system combines external temperature-regulated gonads with an internal network of muscular ducts and secretory glands built to mature and transport gametes. Spermatogenesis runs for ~74 days in the seminiferous tubules, where Sertoli cells nurse dividing germ cells behind the blood–testis barrier; Leydig cells between tubules make testosterone under LH. Sperm mature and are stored in the epididymis, then travel through the vas deferens, which joins the seminal vesicle duct to form the ejaculatory duct crossing the prostate. Seminal fluid from seminal vesicles (fructose), prostate (citrate, PSA) and bulbourethral glands makes up semen. The scrotum keeps the testis ~2 °C below core temperature. Within the human body, the male reproductive system (Organa genitalia masculina) is situated in pelvis, perineum and scrotum, receives arterial perfusion via testicular arteries (abdominal aorta, L2), and is innervated by sympathetic T10–L2 (emission) · parasympathetic S2–S4 (erection).

Structurally, the testis & seminiferous tubules (Testis) comprises 250–300 lobules of coiled seminiferous tubules (total ~250 m) with Sertoli cells and developing germ cells, wrapped in tunica albuginea. Physiologically, the testis & seminiferous tubules governs spermatogenesis and testosterone production. The epididymis is a 6 m coiled duct (head, body, tail) applied to the posterior border of the testis. Physiologically, the epididymis governs sperm maturation, motility acquisition and storage (up to weeks). The vas deferens (Ductus deferens) are a thick-walled 45 cm muscular duct from the epididymal tail, through the inguinal canal into the pelvis. Physiologically, the vas deferens propels sperm by powerful peristalsis at emission. The seminal vesicle (Vesicula seminalis) is a coiled sac behind the bladder whose duct joins the vas to form the ejaculatory duct. Physiologically, the seminal vesicle governs adds ~60% of semen volume: fructose, prostaglandins and clotting proteins. The prostate (Prostata) is a walnut-sized fibromuscular gland around the urethra below the bladder, with peripheral, central and transition zones. Physiologically, the prostate secretes citrate, zinc and PSA that liquefy the seminal coagulum. Structurally, the bulbourethral gland (Glandula bulbourethralis) comprises pea-sized glands (of Cowper) in the deep perineal pouch opening into the spongy urethra. Physiologically, the bulbourethral gland secrete pre-ejaculate mucus that lubricates and neutralises urethral acidity.

Clinically, regarding the testis & seminiferous tubules, undescended testis (cryptorchidism) raises infertility and germ-cell tumour risk; torsion is a 6-hour surgical emergency. From a diagnostic standpoint, in the epididymis, a common site of infection (epididymitis) and of obstruction after vasectomy or infection. In clinical pathology involving the vas deferens, vasectomy divides it for contraception; sperm granulomas may form at the cut ends. Medical evaluation of the seminal vesicle also notes that its fructose is the energy source for sperm and a marker of ejaculatory duct patency.

questions.question: How is sperm produced and transported?
questions.answer: Sperm develop in seminiferous tubules of the testes, mature in the epididymis and pass through the vas deferens and ejaculatory ducts into the urethra. The vas deferens (Ductus deferens) is a thick-walled 45 cm muscular duct from the epididymal tail, through the inguinal canal into the pelvis. Physiologically, the vas deferens propels sperm by powerful peristalsis at emission.

questions.question: What do the prostate and seminal vesicles contribute?
questions.answer: The seminal vesicles and prostate add fluids to semen. Their ducts join the sperm outflow route near the prostate before ejaculation. The seminal vesicle (Vesicula seminalis) is a coiled sac behind the bladder whose duct joins the vas to form the ejaculatory duct. Physiologically, the seminal vesicle governs adds ~60% of semen volume: fructose, prostaglandins and clotting proteins.
